analysis.one_liner: Lets six Northeast states band together to set minimum milk prices above federal levels for their dairy farmers.
analysis.headline: The House never voted: a Judiciary subcommittee deadlocked 5-5 and forwarded the bill without a recommendation, and the 103rd Congress ended with it still in committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would give Congress's consent, which the Constitution requires, to a six-state agreement letting a regional commission set minimum prices for fluid milk above existing federal levels, to keep Northeast dairy farms in business. The higher prices would be paid by milk processors and likely passed to consumers. The bill died in House committee without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Dairy farmers in Vermont, New Hampshire, Maine, Massachusetts, Connecticut, and Rhode Island, who would receive a guaranteed minimum price for fluid milk of up to $1.50 per gallon above federal order levels, adjusted for inflation. Smaller family farms squeezed by falling milk prices gain the most; farmers would also vote on any pricing order by referendum.

how_it_helps.text: Would let a six-state commission set a minimum price for fluid (Class I) milk paid to Northeast dairy farmers, capped at $1.50 per gallon above federal order levels and adjusted annually for inflation, to keep family dairy farms viable.
Requires that any pricing order be approved by at least two-thirds of producers voting in a referendum, with safeguards so individual farmers can vote independently of their cooperatives.
Requires each state's commission delegation to include at least one working dairy farmer and one consumer representative, and caps pricing votes at a two-thirds threshold of state delegations.
Directs the commission to reimburse participants in the WIC nutrition program for the higher milk prices, so low-income mothers and young children are not left to absorb the increase alone.

Explicitly leaves the existing federal milk marketing order system in place, supplementing rather than replacing it, and commits the commission to reimburse the Commodity Credit Corporation for any added federal dairy purchase costs the compact causes.

analysis.who_pays: Milk drinkers and milk handlers in the six compact states. Handlers would be legally required to pay the higher minimum price and an administrative assessment, and those costs are generally passed on to shoppers as higher retail milk prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Northeast milk consumers and milk processors

drawbacks.text: The higher minimum price paid by milk handlers would be passed to consumers as higher retail milk prices across six states, a cost that falls hardest on low-income households, who spend a larger share of their budget on food.

The compact would let six states jointly regulate prices across state lines in a market that spans the region, replacing price competition among milk suppliers with a government-set floor, and could impose compensatory payments on milk shipped in from outside the region.

Only farmers vote in the referendum that approves pricing orders; consumers get one representative per state delegation but no vote, so the people paying the higher prices have little say in setting them.
The $1.50 per gallon ceiling is indexed to inflation and the commission is granted broad, liberally-construed rulemaking power, so the ceiling could climb over time with no new act of Congress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a secure income floor for a few thousand regional dairy farms against a small price increase on a staple for every household in six states. Economists generally expect costs passed through retail channels to exceed what farmers receive, so the total consumer cost would likely outweigh the farm gain, though it would preserve farms, open land, and local milk supply that the region's states said they valued. The design does include real limits: a price ceiling, a producer referendum, consumer seats on the commission, and WIC reimbursement. Whether that trade is worth making is a regional values question that never got debated on the House floor.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Judiciary Committee: a subcommittee split 5-5 and sent it along with no recommendation, and the full committee never acted before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Olver introduced the bill on June 9, 1994 with 21 original cosponsors from the six compact states, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
The bill was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Administrative Law and Governmental Relations on June 16, 1994, which held a hearing on August 3, 1994.
On October 4, 1994, the subcommittee deadlocked 5-5 on the amended bill and forwarded it to the full committee without a recommendation.
The 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 with no full committee vote and no House floor vote on the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Northeast milk drinkers and milk handlers are better off because the bill died: no regional minimum milk price above federal levels took effect through this route. Dairy farmers gained nothing from this bill. Congress ultimately did consent to the same compact in the 1996 farm bill, so this bill's death delayed the higher milk prices by about two years rather than preventing them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Northeast milk drinkers, at least for two years

sides.party_line_note: The only recorded vote was a 5-5 subcommittee tie, so the record does not show a clean party split; sponsorship was bipartisan, with 8 of the 22 cosponsors Republican and one Independent.

industries.industry: Northeast dairy farmers and dairy cooperatives
industries.note: The compact would guarantee these farmers higher prices for fluid milk, with any order approved by a two-thirds producer referendum. The gain comes out of what regional consumers pay at the store, so it is a transfer from milk drinkers to farmers within the region.

Handlers would be legally required to pay the compact's minimum price for fluid milk and an assessment to run the commission. Their resistance to the compact runs alongside consumers' interest in lower milk prices.
The compact could require compensatory payments on fluid milk brought into the regulated region from producers outside it, though the text bars discrimination against out-of-region producers.
